content: Neomycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, has been associated with reports of paralysis following its administration via parenteral injection, topical instillation (such as in orthopedic or abdominal irrigation or local treatment of empyema), and oral use. This risk is particularly heightened when administered shortly after anesthesia or muscle relaxants. If neuromuscular blockade occurs, calcium salts may help reverse the effects, but mechanical respiratory support may be required. Concurrent or sequential use of neurotoxic and/or nephrotoxic drugs, including other aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, paromomycin), should be avoided. Additional drugs to avoid, as listed in aminoglycoside package inserts, include amphotericin B, bacitracin, cephaloridine, cisplatin, colistin, polymyxin B, vancomycin, and viomycin. Potent diuretics, such as ethacrynic acid and furosemide, should also be avoided as they increase the risk of ototoxicity. When administered intravenously, diuretics may enhance aminoglycoside toxicity by altering antibiotic concentrations in serum and tissues. Factors such as advanced age and dehydration further increase the risk of toxicity. Patients with a history of hypersensitivity or serious toxic reactions to other aminoglycosides should exercise caution. Neomycin is contraindicated in patients with inflammatory or ulcerative gastrointestinal disease due to the potential for enhanced gastrointestinal absorption. The risk of hearing loss persists even after discontinuation of the drug. Aminoglycosides cross the placenta, and there have been reports of irreversible bilateral congenital deafness in children whose mothers received streptomycin during pregnancy. Prescribing neomycin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Its use may also lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, particularly fungi, necessitating appropriate therapy if this occurs. Neomycin is rapidly and almost completely absorbed from body surfaces (except the urinary bladder) following local irrigation or topical application during surgical procedures. Delayed-onset, irreversible deafness, renal failure, and death due to neuromuscular blockade have been reported following irrigation of surgical fields with minute quantities of neomycin, regardless of renal function status. Cross-allergenicity among aminoglycosides has been demonstrated, and caution is advised in patients with muscular disorders such as myasthenia gravis or parkinsonism, as these drugs may exacerbate muscle weakness due to their curare-like effects on the neuromuscular junction. Small amounts of orally administered neomycin are absorbed through intact intestinal mucosa. Numerous reports in the literature document nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity associated with oral neomycin use. If renal insufficiency develops during oral therapy, consider reducing the dosage or discontinuing the drug. High oral doses (e.g., 12 g/day) can cause malabsorption syndromes for substances such as fat, nitrogen, cholesterol, carotene, glucose, xylose, lactose, sodium, calcium, cyanocobalamin, and iron. Oral neomycin increases fecal bile acid excretion and reduces intestinal lactase activity. Although serious side effects to the fetus or newborn have not been reported with other aminoglycosides during pregnancy, the potential for harm exists. It is unknown whether neomycin is excreted in human milk, but it has been shown to be excreted in cow milk following a single intramuscular injection. Other aminoglycosides have been shown to be excreted in human milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. Neomycin interferes with bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, thereby reducing the number of ammonia-producing bacteria in the intestine. It is primarily excreted unchanged in feces (97% of the oral dose) and urine (30-50% of the absorbed drug). High doses or prolonged use may impair the absorption of certain nutrients (e.g., iron, vitamins A and B12) and drugs (e.g., digoxin, warfarin). Neomycin may also reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine). This medication is not recommended during pregnancy. While reports of harm in babies born to women using similar drugs exist, the risk may not be the same with neomycin. Breastfeeding is generally considered safe while using this medication, but caution is advised. Neomycin can rarely cause serious kidney problems and nerve damage, leading to permanent hearing loss (including deafness or decreased hearing) and balance issues. These effects may occur even in individuals without pre-existing kidney problems and taking usual doses. Hearing problems may develop long after the drug has been stopped. The risk is higher in older adults, those with kidney disease, or those with severe dehydration. High doses or prolonged use also increase the risk. Careful monitoring by a healthcare provider, including hearing, kidney, and urine tests, can reduce these risks. To minimize the risk of hearing loss and other side effects, take this medication at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration. Do not increase the dose, take it more frequently, or use it for longer than prescribed. If taking neomycin for hepatic encephalopathy, administer it at evenly spaced intervals for optimal effect.
